prime.problem: A GPU is not fast per thread; a single GPU thread adding two arrays runs at 0.04% of the memory's bandwidth, slower than numpy on a laptop. Unless the launch spreads the work across every SM and the data is already on the device, all that hardware sits idle.
prime.fits: Right after the execution model. That card gave you grid, block and thread on paper; here you launch one and watch Harris's T4 ladder go from 1 thread to 1,932×. It is also the first memory-bound kernel, the pattern the coalescing card zooms into.
expect: unified memory page faults and prefetch
prime.goal: Write and launch a correct grid-stride kernel, explain each rung of the 1 → 45× → 1,932× ladder, and know where a CUDA error really comes from.

attend: Why does going from 1 thread to 256 threads give only 45×, not 256×?
Why does going from 1 block to 4,096 blocks give about 43×, and what hardware count does that number match?
What exactly did the unprefetched grid-stride kernel spend its 4.5 ms on, and where did that cost go after prefetching?
Why can an illegal memory access in the kernel be reported at an unrelated cudaMemcpy three lines later?
How does the post's bandwidth figure count bytes, and why is it three arrays and not two?

must: A block never leaves its SM → one block uses 1 of 40 SMs and one SM's memory pipe → 256 threads give 45×, not 256× → many blocks spread over all 40 SMs give another ~43× → then the whole chip is DRAM-bound at 83% of 320 GB/s
Vector add does 1 add per 12 bytes → far below any ridge → the only question is how close you get to peak bandwidth → more math per thread would not help

Unified memory migrates pages on first touch → every page fault stalls the threads that touched it → the kernel ran 95× slower than with prefetch → prefetch moves the copy out of the kernel, but the copy (690 µs) still costs 14.5× the kernel

Launches are asynchronous and return nothing → errors surface at the next call that checks the error state → check cudaGetLastError() after the launch and the sync after, or the report lands somewhere unrelated
elevated: Grid-stride loop (i += blockDim.x * gridDim.x) → any grid size covers any n, i < n doubles as the bounds check, and a warp's accesses stay adjacent → the same pattern returns in reduction kernel 7
reference: the error strings (invalid configuration argument vs invalid argument)
Harris's exact nanosecond timings and the unprefetched first-profile numbers

compress.prompt: Without scrolling up, explain the T4 ladder in 3–5 sentences: why each rung (1 thread, 1 block, many blocks, no prefetch) lands where it does. Or draw it as a chain from "one thread" to "83% of peak" with one cause on each arrow.
checklist: one thread waits on memory for every element: 137 MB/s, 0.04% of peak
one block uses one SM: 45×, still 1.9% of peak
4,096 blocks use all 40 SMs: another ~43×, 265 GB/s = 83% of 320
without prefetch, page faults inside the kernel cost 95×; prefetch moves the copy out but doesn't make it free
vector add is memory-bound, so bandwidth is the only scoreboard

retrieve.q: Explain why a GPU running one thread is slower than numpy on your M3, even though the GPU has 2,560 cores.
answer: one thread uses 1 of 2,560 cores and waits on memory for every element (87.6 ns per element)
numpy streams the arrays near the M3's ~100 GB/s
GPU speed comes from many threads in flight hiding memory latency, not from per-thread speed

retrieve.q: Trace the grid-stride loop for thread 5 of block 3 under <<<4096, 256>>> and under <<<1, 256>>> with N = 1,048,576: its first index, its stride, and how many elements it handles.
answer: 4,096 blocks: index 3 × 256 + 5 = 773, stride 1,048,576, so one element
1 block: there is no block 3; thread 5 starts at 5, stride 256, and handles 4,096 elements
i < n in the loop is the bounds check in both

retrieve.q: Your data starts on the CPU and you add it once. Should you move it to the GPU? Use the card's numbers to decide, and say what changes the answer.
answer: moving 8 MiB of inputs took 690 µs against 47.5 µs of kernel, so for one add, stay on the CPU
the GPU pays off only when data stays resident across many operations
that is exactly the inference-engine case: weights live on the GPU for the whole run

retrieve.q: A kernel launch with <<<512, 2048>>> 'runs' and your program prints garbage but no error. What went wrong, where would a check have caught it, and what would a check right after the launch not tell you?
answer: 2,048 threads per block exceeds the 1,024 limit, so the launch was rejected
cudaGetLastError() right after the launch returns the config error
a clean check after the launch only means it was accepted; runtime faults appear at the next sync or CUDA call

compare.q: On an H100 this vector add's floor is about 3.8 µs, similar to the cost of launching it. Compare "make the kernel faster" with "launch it less often": which lever does each card pull, and which one can still help a kernel that already runs at 83% of peak?
answer: this card: fill the GPU and reach bandwidth, which is already done at 83%
fusion-cuda-graphs: remove launches and DRAM round trips between kernels
at 83% of peak the kernel itself has little left; the remaining time is launch overhead and extra passes over memory, which only fusion or graphs remove

compare.q: The same vector add in CUDA and in Triton tutorial 01: what does each make you write for bounds and indexing, and why do both end up at the same bandwidth?
answer: CUDA: blockIdx × blockDim + threadIdx and an if (or the grid-stride loop)
Triton: pid × BLOCK_SIZE + arange and a boolean mask
both are limited by DRAM bandwidth, and both already coalesce, so there is nothing more to gain

predict.q: Launch the grid-stride kernel with exactly one wave on a T4: <<<160, 256>>> for N = 1,048,576. Commit: how many elements does each thread handle, and should it be much slower than 4,096 blocks?
predict.answer: The stride is 160 × 256 = 40,960, so 1,048,576 = 25 × 40,960 + 24,576: the first 24,576 threads handle 26 elements and the other 16,384 handle 25. It should not be much slower: all 40 SMs are still full (4 blocks × 256 threads each), and each thread now has many independent loads in a row. The time is still set by DRAM bandwidth. That is the point of the grid-stride loop: the grid size stops mattering once it fills the GPU.
